paper.title: Comparison of treatment effects between animal experiments and clinical trials: systematic review
paper.notes: The supplied six-page PDF is the 15 December 2006 Online First source version. Its text and numerical values are retained. The later correction concerns figure-band colour only.

extraction.scope: All substantive scientific content in all six pages of the supplied Online First PDF: six intervention-specific reviews, study-quality table, Figure 1 printed data, all pooled and individually reported estimates, diagnostic tests, study counts, methods, contextual comparisons, limitations, and figures. All graphical point/interval series recoverable from the PDF vector paths are included as approximate digitized collections. Bibliographic numbering, affiliations, legal dates, and administrative numbers are not scientific observations. Underlying cited articles are not separately re-extracted. The external detailed animal-study quality table and web-reference supplement were sought but could not be retrieved.
extraction.notes: Complete extraction of the supplied main PDF, with external-supplement incompleteness declared separately. Exact numerical values repeated in the abstract, results, and discussion are represented once. Digitized values are approximate visual representations, not additional independent evidence or recovered raw study data. Figure 5 lower confidence limits hidden by bars are left unreported rather than inferred. Outcome-specific counts can overlap and must not be added as independent studies.

table_coverage.notes: Both numerical tabular regions in the supplied PDF are fully exported: the six-row study-quality table and the printed five-row data table within Figure 1. The main PDF explicitly refers on page 5 to a detailed animal-experiment quality table at www.crash2.lshtm.ac.uk; direct HTTPS and HTTP access returned 502 on 2026-11-18. That external study-level quality table was not reviewed, so table coverage across the main article and its expressly referenced numerical supplement is incomplete. Separately, the supplementary bibliography w1-w228 (PMC file bmj_39048.407928.BE_1.pdf, labelled References) could not be retrieved; the bibliography is not itself asserted to be an additional numerical table. All supplied main-PDF content was reviewed.

results.title: Head-injury model measurement and translation conditions

source_snippets.text: The grip test measures how long (up to a maximum of 30 seconds) a mouse remains on a taut string suspended between two metal bars. Animals were considered “severely disabled” if they held on for less than five seconds.
The experiments were, however, from one laboratory, had little evidence on adverse effects, and did not examine the influence of comorbidities.
In head injury, treatment was given within five minutes of injury in the animal models but up to eight hours after injury in the clinical trials.

context.model: Weight-drop model in all four grip-test experiments; one laboratory; good allocation concealment and blinded outcome assessment; little adverse-effect evidence; comorbidities not examined.

results.title: Clinical thrombolysis benefit and intracranial-haemorrhage harm

source_snippets.text: Thrombolysis with recombinant tissue plasminogen activator reduces death or dependency after ischaemic stroke, despite an increase in intracranial haemorrhage.

context.evidence_role: Clinical results cited by the review.

results.title: Pooled thrombolysis effect: Infarct volume

source_snippets.text: Tissue plasminogen activator reduced infarct volume by 24% (95% confidence interval 20% to 28%), improved neurobehavioural scores by 23% (17% to 29%), and increased the probability of haemorrhage (odds ratio 1.96, 95% confidence interval 1.63 to 2.35; fig 3).
Infarct volume was reported in 212 comparisons (3301 animals), neurobehavioural scores in 84 (1438 animals), and haemorrhage in 146 (2791 animals).

context.population: Animal models of acute ischaemic stroke
context.intervention: Tissue plasminogen activator or related agents
context.direction: Positive percent improvement favours treatment; haemorrhage OR above 1 indicates harm.

cross_group_summaries.title: Animal–human concordance across six intervention reviews
cross_group_summaries.summary: The authors classify three of six intervention reviews as showing similar animal and clinical outcomes and three as not showing similar outcomes. Thrombolysis and bisphosphonates agree; antenatal corticosteroids agree for respiratory distress but not mortality. Head-injury corticosteroids and tirilazad show discordant efficacy/harm findings; antifibrinolytic animal evidence is insufficient despite clinical benefit.

source_snippets.text: Concordance between animal studies and clinical studies varied for six interventions: three had similar outcomes and three did not.
It would be inappropriate to make general statements about the utility of animal research on the basis of only six interventions.
Lack of concordance between animal experiments and clinical trials may be due to bias, random error, or the failure of animal models to adequately represent human disease

context.interpretation: Author-level categorisation of six selected intervention reviews, not an estimated universal probability of animal–human agreement. Outcome-specific disagreement within a review is retained.
limitations: Only six deliberately selected interventions; no general conclusion about all animal research or mechanistic research.
Incomplete publication and reporting; authors could not rule out unpublished relevant data.
Poor randomisation/blinding reporting, heterogeneous outcomes/designs, and small-study/publication bias.
Some animal models differ from clinical treatment delays, comorbidities, and injury complexity.
implications: Systematic reviews may improve translation and identify model/reporting deficiencies.
Prospective registration could reduce publication bias.
Closer animal–clinical research collaboration and more representative models are proposed, not experimentally tested here.
context.registry_access: Home Office records were requested but not supplied; the authors did not invoke the Freedom of Information Act.

cross_group_summaries.notes: This cross-group summary reuses the six underlying evidence families; it does not create a new independent evidence group.

notes: Six scientific result families follow the six intervention-specific evidence syntheses. The overall concordance conclusion is a cross-group summary. Source tables and digitized figure views preserve provenance and do not create independent evidence. CSV files must accompany this JSON in the same directory.
